title: Secondary Dominants and Tonicization
intro: Any major or minor chord in a key can be made to sound briefly like a tonic by putting its own dominant before it. These secondary dominants (V of V, V of vi …) add chromatic colour and strengthen the pull to their target chord without changing the key.

blocks.text: In C major, V is G. The dominant of G is D (D F♯ A), and D7 (D F♯ A C) is V7/V, read 'five-seven of five'. It contains F♯, which is not in C major: the F♯ acts as a temporary leading tone to G. V/V leads naturally to V, so it usually stands where a predominant chord would: I–V/V–V–I instead of I–ii–V–I.

Every major or minor diatonic chord can be tonicized: V/ii, V/iii, V/IV, V/V and V/vi in major (not V/vii°, because a diminished chord cannot act as a tonic). To build V7/x: find the chord x, go up a perfect fifth from its root, and build a dominant seventh there. In C: V7/ii = A7 (A C♯ E G), V7/iii = B7 (B D♯ F♯ A), V7/IV = C7 (C E G B♭), V7/V = D7, V7/vi = E7 (E G♯ B D).
Secondary leading-tone chords work the same way: vii°7/V in C is F♯°7 (F♯ A C E♭), resolving to G.

A secondary dominant tonicizes its target: for a moment that chord sounds like a tonic. If the music stays in the new key, with a cadence there, it has modulated. The difference is one of length and confirmation; a tonicization lasts a chord or two and the home key carries on.

An accidental that raises a note (or cancels a flat) usually creates a temporary leading tone: look a semitone up for the target's root. In C, F♯ points to G (V/V), C♯ to D (V/ii), G♯ to A (V/vi), D♯ to E (V/iii). A B♭ creates a dominant seventh on C pointing to F (V7/IV). Many standards and pop songs use chains of secondary dominants: E7–A7–D7–G7–C walks round the circle of fifths ('Sweet Georgia Brown', 'Salt Peanuts' bridge).

blocks.title: Spell
blocks.text: In G major, spell V7/V, V7/vi and vii°7/ii.
solution: V of G's V (D) is A: V7/V = A C♯ E G.
vi in G is E minor; its dominant is B: V7/vi = B D♯ F♯ A.
ii in G is A minor; its leading tone is G♯: vii°7/ii = G♯ B D F.

blocks.title: Analyse
blocks.text: In F major a chord A–C♯–E–G resolves to D–F–A. Later a chord F–A–C–E♭ resolves to B♭–D–F. Label both.
solution: D–F–A is vi in F. A7 is its dominant (A is a fifth above D, and C♯ is the leading tone of D): V7/vi.
B♭–D–F is IV in F. F7 is its dominant (F is a fifth above B♭, and E♭ is the 7th, falling to D): V7/IV.
